title: Heme Broadly Promotes Pan-Cancer Resistance to Chemotherapy and Targeted Therapy
content: Background/Objectives: Drug resistance is the dominant factor leading to failure in the treatment of metastatic cancer, accounting for over 90% of cancer deaths. Overcoming drug resistance is highly challenging due to the myriad mechanisms of cancer resistance. Notably, heme strongly promotes tumor development and progression. Heme serves as a prosthetic group for many subunits of mitochondrial respiratory and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) complexes. Furthermore, heme is known to enhance the activities of a wide array of pro-tumorigenic and pro-resistance signal transducers and regulators. Methods: We tested heme’s ability to overcome the anticancer effects of five therapeutic drugs: three widely used chemotherapeutic drugs: docetaxel, carboplatin, and etoposide and two targeted therapeutic drugs: vismodegib and sonidegib. We employed nine cancer cell lines representing diverse types of lungs, breast, and pancreatic cancer. Results: Our study shows that heme, at a physiologically relevant concentration, effectively overcomes the inhibitory effects of chemotherapeutic and targeted therapeutic drugs on the proliferative and survival capabilities of nine representative cancer cell lines. Immunocytochemistry further showed that heme rescues the effects of these anticancer drugs on levels of two crucial mitochondrial regulators, TFAM and OPA1, as well as on the resistance-promoting, activated receptor p-MET. Conclusions: Together, these results show that heme promotes pan-cancer resistance to both chemotherapy and targeted therapy by activating multiple pro-resistance mechanisms. These findings strongly suggest that targeting heme has the potential to overcome the resistance of multiple recalcitrant cancers to commonly applied therapies, including chemotherapy and targeted therapy.
